pages.name: Slope and area
pages.text: A 2000 kg crane trolley speeds up from rest to 0.5 m/s in 2 s. The slope of its speed line is its acceleration, a. So a = 0.5 ÷ 2 = 0.25 m/s². From a start speed u, the speed after a time t is v = u + at. The area under the line is the distance moved, s. The first part is a triangle, ½ × 2 × 0.5 = 0.5 m. The steady part adds 0.5 × 4 = 2 m. Slope and area are the derivative and the integral you know. So by 6 s it has gone 2.5 m.

pages.name: Find the slope
pages.task: A trolley speeds up steadily from rest to 0.6 m/s in 3 s. What is its acceleration?
pages.why: The slope is the rise in speed over the time it took. The speed rises by 0.6 m/s in 3 s. So the acceleration is 0.6 ÷ 3 = 0.2 m/s². Each second, it gains 0.2 m/s.

pages.name: Split the area
pages.text: When the speed doesn't start at zero, split the area. This line rises from 0.5 to 1 m/s in 2 s, at 0.25 m/s². Underneath is a rectangle, ut = 0.5 × 2 = 1 m. That is how far the start speed alone would carry it. On top is a triangle, t wide and a × t tall. Its area is ½at² = ½ × 0.25 × 2² = 0.5 m. That is the extra from speeding up. So s = ut + ½at² = 1.5 m.

pages.task: A trolley at 0.4 m/s brakes steadily to rest in 4 s. How far does it go while braking?
pages.why: The distance is the area under the speed line. Here that area is a triangle, 4 s wide and 0.4 m/s tall. So it is ½ × 4 × 0.4 = 0.8 m. That is the average speed, 0.2 m/s, for 4 s. In symbols, s = ½(u + v)t.

pages.name: No time given
pages.task: No time is given here, so use v² = u² + 2as. A trolley at 0.6 m/s brakes steadily at 0.2 m/s² to rest. How far does it go?
pages.why: From v = u + at, the time is t = (v − u) ÷ a. Put that into s = ½(u + v)t. It gives v² = u² + 2as. Here the end speed v is 0 and u is 0.6. The acceleration a is −0.2, as it slows. So 0 = 0.36 − 0.4 × s. So s = 0.36 ÷ 0.4 = 0.9 m.

pages.text: Here the drive's push is taken away once the trolley is at speed. The lower graph is the [[net force]]: every force along the rail, added up. pages.name: Running steady
pages.task: The trolley runs steady at 0.5 m/s along a level rail. Which is true?
pages.answer: The push equals friction, so the net force is zero
pages.why: Its speed is steady, so its acceleration is zero. So the net force is zero too. Friction holds it back with 100 N. The drive pushes forward with exactly 100 N. The two cancel. It needs no net force to keep moving.

pages.name: The net force graph
pages.text: Here is the whole run with its net force graph. Net force = mass × acceleration. More net force gives more acceleration. More mass gives less. So this graph follows the speed line's slope, not its height. Speeding up at 0.25 m/s² takes 2000 × 0.25 = 500 N. The drive gives 600 N: 500 N net plus the 100 N friction takes. Running steady takes no net force, whatever the speed. Braking takes 500 N the other way. The force graph steps up only while the speed rises, and down only while it falls.

pages.task: The 2000 kg trolley's drive pushes 600 N. Friction holds it back with 100 N. What is its acceleration?
pages.why: Add the forces along the rail. 600 N forward and 100 N back leave 500 N forward. That is the net force. So the acceleration is 500 ÷ 2000 = 0.25 m/s².

pages.name: Impulse and momentum
pages.text: The area under the force graph means something too. While the trolley speeds up, 500 N acts for 2 s. That area, 500 × 2 = 1000 N s, is the [[impulse]]. Force × time = mass × acceleration × time. That is mass × the change in speed. A newton is a kg m/s², so a newton second is a kg m/s. So the impulse gives the trolley 2000 × 0.5 = 1000 kg m/s of [[momentum]]. Momentum is mass × velocity. Velocity and displacement are speed and distance with a direction.

pages.task: A 2000 kg trolley's speed rises steadily from 0.2 to 0.8 m/s in 4 s. What is the net force on it?
pages.why: The speed changes by 0.8 − 0.2 = 0.6 m/s in 4 s. So the acceleration is 0.6 ÷ 4 = 0.15 m/s². The net force is 2000 × 0.15 = 300 N.
